newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania sets new adoption code to curb trafficking.
newsitem.headline: Romania sets new adoption code to curb trafficking.

text.p: Romania's centrist government issued a decree on Wednesday to stop unscrupulous baby-traders making a profit from foreigners seeking to adopt from among the country's 100,000 abandoned children.

State secretary Cristian Tabacaru, head of the Romanian Adoption Committee, said the new rules removed obstacles hampering adoption procedures for foster parents from Romania and abroad but allowed adoptions only through authorised agencies.
"We cut the previous term of six months to 75 days for a child to be declared legally abandoned and free for adoption," he said. "Our interest is for each child to have a family."
Tabacaru said that all adoptions would be supervised by his committee, a government watchdog set up to crack down on trade in babies since Romania opened its borders in 1989.
Foreigners would no longer be allowed to negotiate private, court-approved, adoptions without going through the committee.
The committee, which fears many children are being smuggled out of Romania, has agreements with 34 agencies abroad allowing it to effectively watch over the babies' fate after adoption.

Romania's centrist coalition government, which ended seven years of rule by ex-communists in last year's elections, is overhauling its child protection system to cope with the rising number of children abandoned in state institutions and get rid of its image as a "market for babies".

An average of some 2,500 children have been legally adopted by foreigners annually since the 1989 overthrow of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu shed light on filthy orphanages filled with abandoned children in a country were abortion and contraception were banned.
But aid groups say another 10,000 may have gone illegally -- some to inappropriate, even dangerous, homes.
Local adoptions constantly rose over the past seven years to an average 1,500 children a year, Tabacaru said.
The decree says parents, tutors, legal guardians or others who seek to profit from child adoptions will be punished by up to five years in jail.
"Over the past years, the adoption was seen in Romania strictly as a trade -- something we cannot tolerate," Tabacaru said.
Romanian police have uncovered several child trafficking rings which they said had already managed to "export" dozens of children for prices up to thousands of dollars.
A Romanian court on Tuesday adjourned the trial of Briton John Boast, accused of smuggling a baby girl to Britain.
He is charged with illegal adoption and the alleged purchase for about $60 of another two-year-old gypsy girl taken out of the Balkan country two years ago.
In 1994 a British couple was sentenced to two years and four months in jail for buying and trying to smuggle a baby out of Romania. The president pardoned them.
